title: Rhubarb
description: Species of herbaceous perennial plant with fleshy, sour edible stalks
wiki_lead:
Rhubarb is the fleshy, edible stalks (petioles) of species and hybrids (culinary rhubarb) of Rheum in the family Polygonaceae, which are cooked and used for food. The plant is a herbaceous perennial that grows from short, thick rhizomes. Historically, different plants have been called "rhubarb" in English. The large, triangular leaves contain high levels of oxalic acid and anthrone glycosides, making them poisonous and therefore inedible. The small flowers are grouped in large compound leafy greenish-white to rose-red inflorescences.
The precise origin of culinary rhubarb is unknown. The species Rheum rhabarbarum (syn. R. undulatum) and R. rhaponticum were grown in Europe before the 18th century and used in folk medicine. By the early 18th century, these two species and a possible hybrid of unknown origin, R. × hybridum, were grown as vegetable crops in England and Scandinavia. They readily hybridize, and culinary rhubarb was developed by selecting open-pollinated seed, so its precise origin is almost impossible to determine. In appearance, samples of culinary rhubarb vary on a continuum between R. rhaponticum and R. rhabarbarum. However, modern rhubarb cultivars are tetraploids with 2n = 44, in contrast to 2n = 22 for the wild species.
Rhubarb is a vegetable but is often put to the same culinary uses as fruits. The leaf stalks can be used raw while they have a crisp texture, but are most commonly cooked with sugar and used in pies, crumbles, and other desserts. They have a strong, tart taste. Many cultivars have been developed for human consumption, most of which are recognised as Rheum × hybridum by the Royal Horticultural Society.

Etymology
The word rhubarb is likely to have derived in the 14th century from the Old French rubarbe, which came from the Latin rheubarbarum and Greek rha barbaron, meaning "foreign rha". The Greek physician Dioscorides used the Greek word ῥᾶ (rha), whereas Galen later used ῥῆον (rhēon), Latin rheum. These in turn derive from a Persian name for species of Rheum. The specific epithet rhaponticum, applying to one of the presumed parents of the cultivated plant, means "rha from the region of the Black Sea" or the river Volga, rha being its ancient name.


Cultivation

Rhubarb is grown widely, and with greenhouse production it is available throughout much of the year. It needs rainfall and an annual cold period of up to 7–9 weeks at 3 °C (37 °F), known as 'cold units', to grow well. The plant develops a substantial underground storage organ (rhubarb crowns) and this can be used for early production by transferring field-grown crowns to warm conditions. Rhubarb grown in hothouses (heated greenhouses) is called "hothouse rhubarb", and is typically made available at consumer markets in early spring, before outdoor cultivated rhubarb is available. grok_lead: Rhubarb ( Rheum rhabarbarum) is a hardy perennial vegetable in the Polygonaceae family, native to Siberia and parts of Asia, grown primarily for its thick, tart leaf stalks that are harvested for culinary use in pies, jams, sauces, and other desserts. The plant features large, triangular leaves on long petioles (up to 18 inches) emerging from reddish-brown rhizomes, reaching 2â4 feet in height, with foliage dying back in winter. While the stalks are edible and nutritiousâproviding dietary fiber, vitamin C, calcium, and low calories (about 15 per half-cup serving)âthe leaves contain toxic oxalic acid and must be discarded to avoid nausea, cramps, or more severe effects. Botanically classified as a vegetable, rhubarb is often prepared as a fruit in recipes due to its acidic flavor, which pairs well with sweeteners like sugar or strawberries. Rhubarb's history dates back over 2,000 years to ancient China, where it was first documented in approximately 270 BC for medicinal purposes in texts like the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing, primarily using the rhizomes as a laxative and treatment for digestive issues. Introduced to Europe in the 17th century âreaching Italy in 1608 and broader cultivation by 1638âit transitioned from a medicinal herb to a food crop in the 18th century, with records of its use in British and American tarts and pies from 1778 onward. Today, it remains a staple in cool-climate gardens worldwide, with varieties like Victoria, Crimson Red, and Canada Red selected for stalk color (red or green) and productivity. In cultivation, rhubarb thrives in USDA zones 3â8, requiring cool summers (below 75Â°F average) and winter dormancy (below 40Â°F), along with fertile, well-drained loamy soil enriched with organic matter like compost. Plants are propagated from crowns spaced 3 feet apart in early spring or fall, with harvesting starting in the second or third year and continuing for up to 20 years or more if divided every 4â5 years to prevent overcrowding. Beyond cooking, rhubarb has medicinal applications rooted in traditional Chinese medicine, where species like Rheum palmatum and R. officinale provide anthraquinones (e.g., rhein, emodin) for anti-inflammatory, antibacterial, and anticancer effects, though modern research continues to explore these properties. Its bold foliage also serves ornamental purposes in edible landscapes.
